feedback: If the receiver cannot say what the message meant, point back to the code: 'How did your friend know what your flashes MEANT — what did you agree before you started?'

When a cup-and-string telephone fails, check the string: it must be pulled taut and kept from touching anything to carry the vibration well; a loose string, or one touching something, weakens the sound so much that it may not be heard.

If a message is misunderstood, help the child diagnose before reacting: 'Was the problem what your flash MEANT, or that your friend couldn't see it at all?' A wrong meaning needs the agreed code fixed; a flash genuinely too dim to be seen (or a gap too wide) can legitimately be improved by more brightness or a shorter distance. Judge success at the receiving end — does the message arrive and get decoded correctly — rather than just by how bright or loud the signal is.
After a first failure, prompt the cycle rather than the physics: 'It didn't work the first time — what did you change, and why did that help?'
Success is when the friend correctly receives the intended message, not simply when a light or sound was produced.
activities.intendedInsight: A device communicates only when an agreed code AND a well-built device work together to carry a real message over the distance — communication is sending information, not just producing light or noise.
learnerActions: Name the problem out loud: 'I need to send a message to a friend who is across the room and can't hear me speak.'
Sketch or describe a plan for a device before building it — choose light (a torch signaller), or sound (a cup-and-string telephone or a drum beat pattern).
Build the device from real tools and materials.
Agree a simple shared code with your partner BEFORE sending, e.g. one flash = 'yes', two flashes = 'no', or a drumbeat pattern for an agreed word.
Send the message and check with your partner whether they received the intended meaning correctly.

If it fails, work out WHY before changing something: if the meaning was wrong, fix or clarify the agreed code; if the signal could not be seen or heard at all (e.g. a slack string, or a flash too dim across a wide, bright room), pull the string taut, make the flash brighter, or shorten the gap.
Measure how far apart you can stand and still have the message arrive correctly.
Build or test a second device and compare the two: which carries the message further, and what are the strengths and weaknesses of each?
activities.title: Build and test a real signal device over a distance

feedback: If the child proposes only 'make a light' or 'make a noise', push on meaning: 'How will your friend know what it means?'
Reward ideas that name both a device AND an agreed code.

Treat this as a planning primer — the ideas here should be built and tested for real afterwards; the dialogue can prompt the define/brainstorm phase but does not itself produce a built, tested device.
activities.intendedInsight: Good design starts by clearly defining the problem and the audience, and by planning how the signal will carry a meaning — not just how to make a signal.
learnerActions: Take on a real scenario: an inventor needs to signal a ship at sea, or send a message to a friend across a valley.
Answer the inventor's questions: What problem are we solving? Who needs to receive the message, and why can't we just walk over or shout?
Brainstorm ways light or sound could carry the message — flashes, drumbeats, a string line between two cups.
Answer the pushback: 'How will they know what your flash MEANS?' — propose a code.
Hand off your best idea to the building stage and actually make it.
activities.title: Define and brainstorm the problem with an inventor

feedback: Prompt children to name the code each device uses, not just what it looks like.
Connect each example back to the child's own build: 'Which of these gives you an idea for sending your message?'
Use this as idea-priming background; it shows examples but has no build-and-test loop, so it supports rather than replaces the hands-on making task.
activities.intendedInsight: People across history use many different devices to send information over distance, and each relies on an agreed code — giving ideas for your own design.
learnerActions: Look at real communication devices one at a time: cup-and-string telephone, lighthouse, drum, semaphore flags, bell.
For each, work out how it sends a signal far away and what 'code' it uses — flashes, beats, flag positions, rings.
Play a 'what message is this sending?' guessing game for a given signal.
Use the examples to spark ideas for your own device and code.
activities.title: Explore real communication devices and their codes

feedback: Confirm that a string telephone works with a TAUT string; a slack string does not carry the vibration.
If the design steps are ordered wrong, re-run the sequence pointing back to the last build the child actually did, and note that after 'improve' you often loop back to test again.

Treat this as a light knowledge check: it can confirm recognition of the step order and light-vs-sound sorting, but it does not elicit the independent construction of a working device, so it supplements rather than replaces building and testing.
activities.intendedInsight: The design process has a usual working order and is iterative (you loop back to improve), and different devices rely on light or on sound to carry a signal.
learnerActions: Put the design steps in order: define → plan → build → test → improve.
Sort devices into 'uses light' versus 'uses sound'.
Answer: 'What makes a string telephone work — a taut string or a slack string?' (Correct answer: taut.)
activities.title: Quick check on design steps and signal types
